prompt: According to valence bond theory, how does a covalent bond form?

choices.text: A singly occupied orbital on one atom overlaps a singly occupied orbital on another
A filled orbital on one atom overlaps a filled orbital on another
choices.why: Each overlapping orbital brings one electron, so together they hold the bonding pair. Two filled orbitals would hold four electrons.

choices.text: One atom transfers an electron to the other
choices.why: Electron transfer makes ions. In valence bond theory the electrons are shared in overlapping orbitals.

choices.text: Atomic orbitals combine into new orbitals belonging to the whole molecule
choices.why: That is the molecular orbital picture (Section 1.11), not valence bond theory.

explanation: In valence bond theory, a covalent bond forms when two atoms approach closely and a singly occupied orbital on one overlaps a singly occupied orbital on the other. The electrons are then paired in the overlapping orbitals and attracted to both nuclei.

prompt: In valence bond theory, which orbitals overlap to form the H–H bond in H2?

choices.text: Two singly occupied hydrogen 1s orbitals
Two hydrogen 2p orbitals
choices.why: A hydrogen atom's one electron is in its 1s orbital, and that's the orbital that overlaps.

choices.text: A hydrogen 1s orbital and a hydrogen 2s orbital
choices.why: Both hydrogen atoms use their 1s orbitals.

choices.text: Two sp3 hybrid orbitals
choices.why: Hybrid orbitals come in with carbon and other second-row atoms; hydrogen uses its 1s orbital.

explanation: In the H2 molecule, the H–H bond results from the overlap of two singly occupied hydrogen 1s orbitals.

choices.text: A bond formed by head-on overlap of two atomic orbitals along the line between the nuclei
A bond formed by sideways overlap of two p orbitals
choices.why: That is a pi (π) bond, met in Section 1.8.

choices.text: A bond with electron density above and below the line between the nuclei
choices.why: That describes a π bond; a σ bond's electrons are centered on the line between the nuclei.

choices.text: Any bond between two hydrogen atoms
choices.why: H–H is one example, but σ bonds are defined by head-on overlap, and they occur between many atoms.

explanation: Bonds formed by the head-on overlap of two atomic orbitals along a line drawn between the nuclei are called sigma (σ) bonds. They are cylindrically symmetrical.

prompt: If a plane cut through the middle of the H–H σ bond, perpendicular to the bond, what shape would the cross-section of the overlapping orbitals be?

choices.text: A circle
A dumbbell
choices.why: The overlapping orbitals are egg-shaped along the bond, and a slice across a cylindrically symmetrical bond is round.

choices.text: A square
choices.why: The bond is cylindrically symmetrical, so its cross-section is a circle.

choices.text: Two separate lobes
choices.why: A slice across a σ bond gives one round region, not two lobes.

explanation: The overlapping orbitals in H2 have an elongated egg shape. A plane through the middle of the bond meets them in a circle: the H–H bond is cylindrically symmetrical, the mark of a σ bond.

prompt: What is the bond strength of the H–H bond, in kJ/mol?
explanation: 436 kJ/mol (104 kcal/mol) of energy is released when two H atoms form H2, so the H–H bond strength is 436 kJ/mol. The same amount must be put in to break the bond.

prompt: The H–H bond strength is 436 kJ/mol. What is that in kcal/mol? (1 kJ = 0.2390 kcal)
explanation: 436 kJ/mol × 0.2390 kcal/kJ = 104.2 kcal/mol, which the book rounds to 104 kcal/mol.

prompt: A bond strength is given as 104 kcal/mol. What is it in kJ/mol? (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ)
explanation: 104 kcal/mol × 4.184 kJ/kcal = 435.1 kJ/mol, essentially the H–H bond strength of 436 kJ/mol.

prompt: How much energy is needed to break all the H–H bonds in 2.00 mol of H2? (H–H bond strength: 436 kJ/mol)
explanation: Each mole of H–H bonds needs 436 kJ to break, so 2.00 mol needs 2.00 × 436 kJ = 872 kJ.

prompt: How does the energy of an H2 molecule compare with the energy of two separate H atoms?

choices.text: H2 is 436 kJ/mol lower in energy, so it is more stable
H2 is 436 kJ/mol higher in energy
choices.why: Energy is released when the bond forms, so H2 is lower in energy than the separate atoms.

choices.text: They have the same energy
choices.why: The bond-forming reaction 2H· → H2 releases 436 kJ/mol, so the energies differ.

choices.text: H2 is lower in energy, but only by 74 kJ/mol
choices.why: 74 is the H–H bond length in pm. The energy difference is 436 kJ/mol.

explanation: During 2H· → H2, 436 kJ/mol of energy is released. The H2 molecule has 436 kJ/mol less energy than the two H atoms, so it is more stable.

prompt: What is the bond length of the H–H bond, in picometers?
explanation: The optimum distance between the two nuclei, the bond length, is 74 pm in the H2 molecule.

prompt: What would happen if the two nuclei of H2 came much closer than the bond length?

choices.text: They would repel each other, because both are positively charged
They would form a stronger bond
choices.why: Too close, and the positive nuclei repel; the bond is most stable at the bond length.

choices.text: They would share more electrons
choices.why: There are still only two bonding electrons; moving the nuclei closer just increases their repulsion.

choices.text: Nothing; any distance shorter than the bond length is equally stable
choices.why: Energy rises again at short distances, because the nuclei repel.

explanation: If the nuclei are too close, they repel each other because both are positively charged; if they are too far apart, they can't share the bonding electrons. The bond length is the distance between these extremes.

prompt: Why can't the two H atoms in H2 be stable much farther apart than the bond length?

choices.text: They would be too far apart to share the bonding electrons
Their nuclei would repel each other
choices.why: Repulsion is the problem when nuclei are too close, not too far apart.

choices.text: Their electrons would have to have the same spin
choices.why: The issue is distance: far apart, the orbitals no longer overlap to share electrons.

choices.text: The atoms would become ions
choices.why: Pulling the atoms apart gives two neutral H atoms, not ions.

explanation: If the nuclei are too far apart, they won't be able to share the bonding electrons. There is an optimum distance between nuclei that gives maximum stability.

prompt: On a plot of energy against the distance between two hydrogen nuclei, where is the bond length?

choices.text: At the distance where the energy is at its minimum
At the distance where the energy is highest
choices.why: The highest energies are at very short distances, where the nuclei repel. The bond length is at the lowest point.

choices.text: Where the energy reaches zero
choices.why: The curve's low point is below zero; the bond length is at that minimum.

choices.text: At the largest distance on the plot
choices.why: At large distances the atoms barely interact. The bond length is where they are most stable.

explanation: The distance between nuclei at the minimum-energy point of the energy curve is the bond length: 74 pm for H2. Every covalent bond has a characteristic bond strength and bond length.

prompt: Which model of covalent bonding is more easily visualized, and so is used for most descriptions in this book?

choices.text: Valence bond theory
Molecular orbital theory
choices.why: MO theory is the other model, described in Section 1.11. Valence bond theory is the more easily visualized of the two.

choices.text: Ionic bonding theory
choices.why: The two models of covalent bonding are valence bond theory and molecular orbital theory.

choices.text: The octet rule alone
choices.why: The octet rule predicts how many bonds form; the two bonding models describe how sharing forms them.

explanation: Two models describe covalent bonding: valence bond theory and molecular orbital theory. Valence bond theory is the more easily visualized, so most descriptions in the book derive from it.

prompt: In valence bond theory, once two orbitals overlap to form a bond, what holds the atoms together?

choices.text: The paired electrons in the overlapping orbitals are attracted to both nuclei
The two nuclei attract each other
choices.why: Both nuclei are positive and repel each other; the shared electrons hold them together.

choices.text: Each electron stays attracted only to its own nucleus
choices.why: The paired electrons are attracted to both nuclei, which bonds the atoms.

choices.text: The electrons are transferred to one atom
choices.why: In a covalent bond the electrons are shared, not transferred.

explanation: When the singly occupied orbitals overlap, the electrons are paired in the overlapping orbitals and are attracted to the nuclei of both atoms, thus bonding the atoms together.
